children.translated_text: <s>Dharmakīrti</s>: <s>Nyāyabindu Prakaraṇakārikā</s> (Treatise on the Drop of Logic — The Sūtra Text)
1. First Chapter: Examination of Direct Perception (<s>pratyakṣaparicchedaḥ</s>)

children.text:
1/1 samyagjñānapūrvikā sarvapuruṣārthasiddhiriti tadvayutpādayate /
1/2 dvividhaṃ samyagjñānam /
1/3 pratyakṣam, anumānaṃ ceti /
1/4 tatra pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍhamabhrāntam /
1/5 abhilāpasaṃsargayogyapratibhāsapratītiḥ kalpanā
1/6 tayā rahitaṃ timirāśubhramaṇanauyānasambhramādyanāhitavibhramaṃ jñānaṃ pratyakṣam /
1/7 taccaturvidham /
1/8 indriyajñānam / (1)
1/9 svaviṣayānantaraviṣayasahakāriṇendriyajñānena samanantarapratyayena janitaṃ tanmanovijñānam / (2)
1/10 sarvacittacaittānāmātmasaṃvedanam / (3)
1/11 bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajaṃ yogijñānaṃ ceti / (4)
1/12 tasya viṣayaḥ svalakṣaṇam /
1/13 yasyārthasya sannidhānāsannidhānābhyāṃ jñānapratibhāsabhedastatsvalakṣaṇam /
1/14 tadeva paramārthasat /
1/15 arthakriyāsāmarthyalakṣaṇatvād vastunaḥ /
1/16 anyat sāmānyalakṣaṇam
1/17 so 'numānasya viṣayaḥ /
1/18 atdeva ca pratyakṣaṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇaphalam /
1/19 arthapratītirūpatvāt /
1/20 arthasārūpyamasya pramāṇam /
1/21 tadvaśādarthapratītisiddhareti /
children.translated_text:
1/1 The accomplishment of all human purposes is preceded by correct knowledge (<s>samyagjñāna</s>) — this [treatise] generates [the understanding of] that.
1/2 Correct knowledge is of two kinds.
1/3 [Namely,] direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>).
1/4 Among these, direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) is free from conceptual construction (<s>kalpanāpoḍha</s>) and non-erroneous (<s>abhrānta</s>).
1/5 <s>Kalpanā</s> (conceptual construction) is a cognition that appears [as an object] capable of being associated with verbal expression.
1/6 Knowledge free from that, [and] not vitiated by distortion caused by floaters in the eye (<s>timira</s>), rapid motion, movement on a boat, [or other] disturbances, is direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>).
1/7 It is of four kinds:
1/8 (1) Sense cognition (<s>indriyajñāna</s>);
1/9 (2) Mental cognition (<s>manovijñāna</s>) produced by sense cognition — [which takes] its own object and the immediately preceding object as its cooperating condition, with sense cognition as the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>);
1/10 (3) Self-awareness (<s>ātmasaṃvedana</s>) of all mental and mental-concomitant [states];
1/11 (4) And the knowledge of a yogin (<s>yogijñāna</s>), born at the culmination of intense meditation on a real object (<s>bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyanta</s>).
1/12 Its object is the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>).
1/13 That [thing] whose cognition-appearance differs according to the presence or absence [of the object] is the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>).
1/14 That alone is ultimately real (<s>paramārthasat</s>),
1/15 because the real thing (<s>vastu</s>) is characterized by its causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāsāmarthya</s>).
1/16 The other [kind of object] is the universal (<s>sāmānyalakṣaṇa</s>);
1/17 that is the object of inference (<s>anumāna</s>).
1/18 And direct knowledge itself is the result of a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇaphala</s>),
1/19 because it has the form of the apprehension of an object (<s>arthapratīti</s>).
1/20 Its correspondence to the object (<s>arthasārūpya</s>) is the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>);
1/21 because the apprehension of the object is established by virtue of that.
Thus [ends] the first chapter, the Examination of Direct Perception.
Second Chapter: Examination of Inference for Oneself (<s>svārthānumānaparicchedaḥ</s>)

children.text:
2/1 anumānaṃ dvidhā /
2/2 svārtha parārtha ca /
2/3 tatra svārtha trirūpālliṅgād yadanumeye jñānaṃ tadanumānam /
2/4 pramāṇalakṣaṇavyavasthātrāpi pūrvavat /
2/5 trairūpyaṃ punarliṅgasyānumeye sattvameva, sapakṣa eva sattvam, asapakṣe cāsattvameva niścitam /
2/6 anumeyo 'tra jijñāsitaviśeṣo dharmī /
2/7 sādhyadharmasāmānyena samāno 'rthaḥ sapakṣa /
2/8 na sapakṣo 'sapakṣaḥ /
2/9 tato 'nyastadviruddhastadabhāvaśceti
2/10 trirūpāṇi ca trīṇyeva liṅgāni /
2/11 anupalabdhiḥ svabhāvaḥ kārya ceti /
2/12 tatrānupalabdhiryathā- na pradeśaviśeṣe kvacid ghaṭaḥ, upalabdhikṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdheriti /
2/13 upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptirūpalambhapratyayāntarasākalyaṃ svabhāvaviśeṣaśca /
2/14 yaḥ svabhāvaḥ satsvanyeṣūṣalambhapratyayeṣu san pratyakṣa eva bhavati, sa svabhāvaviśeṣaḥ /
2/15 svabhāvaḥ svasattāmātraprabhāvini sādhyadharme hetuḥ /
2/16 yathā- vṛkṣo 'yaṃ śiśapātvāditi /
2/17 kārya yathā- bahniratra dhūmāditi /
2/18 atra dvau vastusādhanau / ekaḥ pratiṣedhahetuḥ /
2/19 svabhāvapratibandhe hi satyartho 'rtha gamayet /
2/20 tadapratibaddhasya tadavyabhicāraniyamābhāvāt /
2/21 sa ca pratibandhaḥ sādhye 'rthe liṅgasya /
2/22 vastutastādātmyāt tadutpatteśca /
2/23 atatsvabhāvasyātadutpatteśca tatrāpratibaddhasvabhāvatvāt /
2/24 te ca tādātmyatadutpattī svabhāvakāryayoreveti tābhyāmeva vastusiddhiḥ /
2/25 pratiṣedhasiddhirapi yathoktāyā evānupalabdheḥ /
2/26 sati vastuni tasyā asambhavāt /
2/27 anyathā cānupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpteṣu deśakālasvabhāvaviprakṛṣṭeṣvartheṣvātmapratyakṣanivṛtterabhavaniścayābhāvāt /
2/28 amūḍhasmṛtisaṃskārasyātītasya vartamānasya ca pratipattṛpratyakṣasya nivṛttirabhāvavyavahāraprasādhanī /
2/29 tasyā evābhāvaniścayāt /
2/30 sā ca prayogabhedādekādaśaprakārā /
2/31 svabhāvānupalabdhiryathā- nātra dhūma upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdheriti / (1)
2/32 kāryānupalabdhiryathā- nātrāpratibaddhasāmarthyāni dhūmakāraṇāni santi, dhūmābhāvāditi / (2)
2/33 vyāpakānupalabdhiryathā- nātra śiśapā, vṛkṣābhāvāditi / (3)
2/34 svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhiryathā- nātra śītasparśo vahneriti / (4)
2/35 viruddhakāryopalabdhiryathā- nātra śītasparśo dhūmāditi / (5)
2/36 viruddhavyāptopalabdhiryathā- na dhruvabhāvī bhūtasyāpi bhāvasya vināśaḥ, hetvantarāpekṣaṇāditi / (6)
2/37 kāryaviruddhopalabdhiryathā- nehāpratilbaddhasāmarthyāni śītakāraṇāni santi, vahneriti / (7)
2/38 vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhiryathā- nātra tuṣāraspaśo vahneriti / (8)
2/39 kāraṇānupalabdhiryathā- nātra dhūmo vahnyabhāvāditi / (9)
2/40 kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhiryathā- nāsya romaharṣādiviśeṣāḥ, sannihitadahanaviśeṣatvāditi / (10)
2/41 kāraṇaviruddhakāyapilabdhiryathā- na romaharṣādiviśeṣayuktapuruṣāvānayaṃ pradeśaḥ, dhūmāditi / (11)
2/42 ime sarve kāryānupalabdhyādayo daśānupalabdhiprayogāḥ svabhāvānupalabdhau saṃgrahamupayānti /
2/43 pāramparyeṇārthāntaravidhipratiṣedhābhyāṃ prayogabhede 'pi /
2/44 prayogadarśanābhyāsāt svayamapyevaṃ vyavacchedapratītirbhavati svārthe 'pyanumāne 'syāḥ prayoganirdeśaḥ /
2/45 sarvatra cāsyāmabhāvavyavahārasādhanyāmanupalabdhau yeṣāṃ svabhāvaviruddhadīnāmupalabdhyā kāraṇādīnāmanupalabdhyā ca pratiṣedha uktasteṣāmupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānāmevipalabdhiśca veditavyā /
2/46 anyeṣāṃ virodhakāryakāraṇabhāvāsiddheḥ /
2/47 viprakṛṣṭaviṣayā punaranupalabdhiḥ pratyakṣānumānanivṛttilakṣaṇā saṃśayahetuḥ /
2/48 pramāṇanivṛttāvapyarthābhāvāsiddheriti /
children.translated_text:
2/1 <s>Anumāna</s> (inference) is twofold.
2/2 (Namely,) <s>svārtha</s> (inference for oneself) and <s>parārtha</s> (inference for others).
2/3 Of these, <s>svārtha</s> (inference for oneself) is the cognition that arises regarding the <s>anumeya</s> (object to be inferred) from a <s>liṅga</s> (logical mark) possessing the three characteristics; that is <s>anumāna</s> (inference).
2/4 The determination of its status as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) is as before (i.e., as stated for perception).
2/5 The three characteristics of the <s>liṅga</s> (logical mark) are: its presence only in the <s>anumeya</s> (inferential subject), its presence only in the <s>sapakṣa</s> (homologous instances), and its ascertained absence only in the <s>asapakṣa</s> (heterologous instances).
2/6 The <s>anumeya</s> (inferential subject) here is the <s>dharmin</s> (property-possessor) whose specific property is under inquiry.
2/7 <s>Sapakṣa</s> (the homologous instance) is an object that is similar (to the inferential subject) by sharing the general property to be established.
2/8 What is not <s>sapakṣa</s> is <s>asapakṣa</s> (the heterologous instance).
2/9 That which is different from it, that which is contradictory to it, and that which is the absence of it —
2/10 The <s>liṅgas</s> (logical marks) possessing the three characteristics are exactly three.
2/11 (They are:) <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension), <s>svabhāva</s> (essential nature), and <s>kārya</s> (effect).
2/12 Of these, <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension) is, for example: "There is no pot in this particular location, because of the non-apprehension of what fulfills the conditions for apprehension."
2/13 Fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension means the completeness of the other conditions for perception and a specific essential nature (i.e., the object must be perceptible).
2/14 That essential nature which, when the other conditions for perception are present, is directly perceptible — that is the specific essential nature.
2/15 <s>Svabhāva</s> (essential nature) is a <s>hetu</s> (logical reason) for the <s>sādhyadharma</s> (property to be established) that arises from the mere fact of its own existence.
2/16 For example: "This is a tree, because it is a <s>śiṃśapā</s> (Dalbergia sissoo)."
2/17 <s>Kārya</s> (effect) is, for example: "There is fire here, because of smoke."
2/18 Of these, two establish a positive entity; one is a reason for negation.
2/19 For only when there is an essential connection (<s>svabhāvapratibandha</s>) can one thing lead to (the cognition of) another.
2/20 Because for that which is not so connected, there is no necessity of non-deviation from it.
2/21 And that connection is the connection of the <s>liṅga</s> (logical mark) with the <s>sādhya</s> (object to be established).
2/22 In reality, (this connection is) through essential identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) or through causal origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>).
2/23 Because that which does not have that nature and does not originate from it has a nature that is not connected to it.
2/24 And those two — essential identity and causal origination — belong only to the essential nature and the effect, respectively; therefore, establishment of a positive entity is only through these two.
2/25 Establishment of negation also (comes) from the very non-apprehension that has been described.
2/26 Because when the entity exists, its (non-apprehension) is impossible.
2/27 And otherwise, in the case of objects that are remote in space, time, or nature — which do fulfill the conditions for apprehension — since there is no cessation of one's own perception, there would be no ascertainment of absence.
2/28 The cessation of the perception of an unconfused perceiver whose memory-impressions are intact, regarding the past and the present, is what establishes the convention of absence.
2/29 Because there is ascertainment of absence from that (cessation of perception) alone.
2/30 And this (non-apprehension) is of eleven types, through differences in application.
2/31 Non-apprehension of the essential nature (<s>svabhāvānupalabdhi</s>), for example: "There is no smoke here, because of the non-apprehension of what fulfills the conditions for apprehension." (1)
2/32 Non-apprehension of the effect (<s>kāryānupalabdhi</s>), for example: "There are no causes of smoke here with unobstructed capacity, because of the absence of smoke." (2)
2/33 Non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>), for example: "There is no <s>śiṃśapā</s> here, because of the absence of a tree." (3)
2/34 Apprehension of what is contradictory in essential nature (<s>svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi</s>), for example: "There is no cold touch here, because of fire." (4)
2/35 Apprehension of the effect of what is contradictory (<s>viruddhakāryopalabdhi</s>), for example: "There is no cold touch here, because of smoke." (5)
2/36 Apprehension of what is pervaded by the contradictory (<s>viruddhavyāptopalabdhi</s>), for example: "The destruction of an existent entity is not of permanent nature, because it depends on another cause." (6)
2/37 Apprehension of the effect of what is contradictory to the effect (<s>kāryaviruddhopalabdhi</s>), for example: "There are no causes of cold here with unobstructed capacity, because of fire." (7)
2/38 Apprehension of what is contradictory to the pervader (<s>vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi</s>), for example: "There is no frost-touch here, because of fire." (8)
2/39 Non-apprehension of the cause (<s>kāraṇānupalabdhi</s>), for example: "There is no smoke here, because of the absence of fire." (9)
2/40 Apprehension of what is contradictory to the cause (<s>kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi</s>), for example: "This (person) does not have the specific characteristics of horripilation etc., because of the proximity of a specific fire." (10)
2/41 Apprehension of the effect of what is contradictory to the cause (<s>kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi</s>), for example: "This location is not one containing a person with the specific characteristics of horripilation etc., because of smoke." (11)
2/42 All these ten types of non-apprehension applications — from non-apprehension of the effect onward — are subsumed under non-apprehension of the essential nature.
2/43 Even though the applications differ, (they are subsumed) through the indirect positive and negative establishment of other things.
2/44 Through repeated observation of (these) applications, such discriminative cognition arises by itself even in <s>svārtha</s> (inference for oneself); (yet) the exposition of the application is (given here for completeness).
2/45 And in all cases of this non-apprehension which establishes the convention of absence, the apprehension of those things contradictory in essential nature, etc., and the non-apprehension of causes, etc., by which negation has been stated — their apprehension should be understood as (the apprehension) of those fulfilling the conditions for apprehension.
2/46 Because for others, the establishment of contradiction, effect-cause relation, etc. is not possible.
2/47 Furthermore, non-apprehension pertaining to remote objects — characterized by the cessation of perception and inference — is a cause of doubt.
2/48 Because even when the <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) has ceased, the absence of the object is not established.
Thus [ends] the second chapter, the Examination of Inference for Oneself (<s>svārthānumānaparicchedaḥ</s>).
Third Chapter: Examination of Inference for Others (<s>parārthānumānaparicchedaḥ</s>)

children.text:
3/1 trirūpaliṅgākhyānaṃ parārthamanumānam /
3/2 kāraṇe kāryopacārāt /
3/3 tad dvividham /
3/4 prayogabhedāt /
3/5 sādhamyavadvaidhamyavacca /
3/6 nānāyorarthataḥ kaścid bhedaḥ /
3/7 anyatra prayogabhedāt /
3/8 tatra sādharmyavatprayogaḥ- yadupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptaṃ sannopalabhyate so 'sad vyavahāraviṣayaḥ siddhaḥ / yathā- anyo dṛṣṭaḥ kaścid śaśaviṣāṇādiḥ / nopalabhyate ca kvacit pradeśaviśeṣe upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpo ghaṭa ityanupalabdhiprayogaḥ /
3/9 tathā svabhāvahetoḥ prayogaḥ- yat sat tat sarvamanityam, yathā ghaṭādiriti śuddhasya svabhāvahetoḥ prayogaḥ /
3/10 yadutpattimat tadanityamiti svabhāvabhūtadharmabhedena svabhāvasya prayogaḥ /
3/11 yat kṛtakaṃ tadanityamityupādhibhedena /
3/12 apekṣitaparavyāpāro hi bhāvaḥ svabhāvaniṣpattau kṛtaka iti /
3/13 evaṃ prayatnāntarīyaka- pratyayabhedabheditvādayo 'pi draṣṭavyāḥ /
3/14 sannutpattimān kṛtako vā śabda iti pakṣadharmopadarśanam /
3/15 sarva ete sādhanadharmā yathāsvaṃ pramāṇaiḥ siddhasādhanadharmamātrānubandhe eva sādhyadharme 'vagantavyāḥ /
3/16 tasyaiva tatsvabhāvatvāt /
3/17 svabhāvasya ca hetutvāt /
3/18 vastutastayostādātmyam /
3/19 tanniṣpattāvaniṣpannasya tatsvabhāvatvābhāvāt /
3/20 vyabhicārasambhavācca /
3/21 kāryahetoḥ prayogaḥ - yatra dhūmastatrāgniḥ / yathā mahānasādau / asti ceha dhūma iti /
3/22 ihāpi siddhe eva kāryakāraṇabhāve kāraṇe sādhye kāryaheturvaktavyaḥ /
3/23 vaidharmyavataḥ prayogaḥ- yat sadupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptaṃ tadupalabhyata eva / yathā nīlādiviśeṣaḥ / na caivamihopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya sata upalabdhirghaṭasyetyanupalabdhiprayogaḥ /
3/24 asatyanityatve, nāsti sattvamutpattimattvaṃ kṛtakatvaṃ vā / saṃśca śabda utpattimān kṛtako veti svabhāvahetoḥ prayogaḥ /
3/25 asatyagnau na bhavatyeva dhūmaḥ / atra cāsti dhūma iti kāryahetoḥ prayogaḥ /
3/26 sādharmyeṇāpi hi prayoge 'rthād vaidharmyagatiriti /
3/27 asati tasmin sādhyena hetoranvayābhāvāt /
3/28 tathā vaidharmyeṇāpyanvayagatiḥ /
3/29 asati tasmin sādhyābhāve hetvabhāvasyāsiddheḥ /
3/30 nahi svabhāvapratibandhe 'satyekasya nivṛttāvaparasya niyamena nivṛttiḥ /
3/31 sa ca dviprakāraḥ- sarvasya tādātmyalakṣaṇastadutpatilakṣaṇaścetyuktam /
3/32 tena hi nivṛtti kathayatā pratibandho darśanīyaḥ / tasmāt nivṛttivacanamākṣiptapratibandhopadarśanameva bhavati / yacca pratibandhopadarśanaṃ tadevānvayavacanamityekenāpi vākyenānvayamukhena vyatirekamukhena vā prayuktena sapakṣāsapakṣayorliṅgasya sadasattvakhyāpanaṃ kṛtaṃ bhavatīti nāvaśayaṃ vākyadvayaprayogaḥ /
3/33 anupalabdhāvapi - yat sad upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptaṃtadupalabhyata evetyukte, anupalabhyamānaṃ tādṛśamasaditi pratīreranvayasiddhiḥ /
3/34 dvayorapyanayoḥ prayogayornāvaśyaṃ pakṣanirdeśaḥ /
3/35 yasmāt sādharmyavatprayoge 'pi yadupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptaṃ sannopalabhyate, so 'sadvayavahāraviṣayaḥ / nopalabhyate cātropalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpto ghaṭa ityukte sāmarthyādeva neha ghaṭa iti bhavati /
3/36 tathā vaidharmyavatprayoge 'pi- yaḥ sad vyavahāraviṣaya upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptaḥ sa upalabhyata eva / na tathātra tādṛśo ghaṭa upalabhyate- ityukte sāmarthyādeva neha sadvayavahāraviṣaya iti bhavati /
3/37 kīdṛśaḥ punaḥ pakṣa iti nirdeśyaḥ?
3/38 svarūpeṇaiva svayamiṣṭo 'nirākṛtaḥ pakṣa iti /
3/39 svarūpeṇeti sādhyatveneṣṭaḥ /
3/40 svarūpeṇaiveti sādhyatvenaiveṣṭo na sādhanatvenāpi /
3/41 yathā śabdasyānityatve sādhye cākṣuṣatvaṃ hetuḥ, śabde 'siddhatvāt sādhyaṃ bhavatīti na punastadiha sādhyatvenaiveṣṭam, sādhanatvenāpyabhidhānāt /
3/42 svayamiti vādinā /
3/43 yastadā sādhanamāha /
3/44 etena yadyapi kvacicchāstre sthitaḥ sādhanamāha, tacchāstrakāreṇa tasmin dharmiṇyanekadharmābhyupagame 'pi yastadā tena vādinā dharmaḥ svayaṃ sādhayitu miṣṭaḥ sa eva sādhyo netara ityuktaṃ bhavati /
3/45 iṣṭa iti yatrārthe vivādena sādhanamupanyastaṃ tasya siddhimicchatā so 'nukto 'pi vacanena sādhyo bhavati /
3/46 tadadhikaraṇatvād vivādasya /
3/47 yathā parārthāścakṣurādayaḥ saṅghātatvācchayanāsanādyaṅgavaditi / atrātmārthā ityanuktāvapyātmārthataiva sādhyā / tena noktamātrameva sādhyam- ityuktaṃ bhavati /

3/126 tathānanvayo 'pradarśitānvayaśca / yathā- yo vaktā sa rāgādimān, iṣṭapuruṣavat / anityaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvād ghaṭavaditi /
3/127 tathā viparītānvayaḥ- yadanityaṃ tat kṛtakamiti /
3/128 sādharmyeṇa dṛṣṭāntadoṣāḥ /
3/129 vaidharmyeṇāpi- paramāṇuvat karmavad ākāśavaditi sādhyādyavyatirekiṇaḥ /
3/130 tathā sandigdhasādhyavyatirekādayaḥ / yathā- asarvajñāḥ kapilādayo 'nāptā vā avidyamānasarvajñatāptatāliṅgabhutapramāṇātiśayaśāsanatvāditi / atra vaidharmyodāharaṇam- yaḥ sarvajña āpto vā sa jyotirjñānādikamu padiṣṭavān / yathā- ṛṣabhavardhamānādiriti / tatrāsarvajñatānāptatayoḥ sādhyadharmayoḥ sandigdho vyatirekaḥ /
3/131 sandigdhasādhanavatireko yathā- na trayividā brāhmaṇe grāhyavacana kaścid vivikṣitaḥ puruṣo rāgādimattvāditi / atra vedharmyodāharaṇam- ye grāhyavacanā na te rāgādimantaḥ, tadyathā gautamādayo dharmaśāstrāṇāṃ praṇetāra iti / gautamādibhyo rāgādimattvasya sādhanadharmasya vyāvṛttiḥ sandigdhā /
3/132 sandigdhobhayavyatireko yathā- avitarāgāḥ kapilādayaḥ, parigrahāgrahayogāditi / atra vaidharmyaṇodāharanam- yo vītarāgo na tasya parigrahāgraha, yatharṣabhāderiti / ṛṣabhāderavītarāgatvaparigrahāgrahayogayoḥ sādhyasādhanadharmayoḥ sandigdho vyatiraikaḥ /
3/133 avyatireko yathā- avītarāgo 'yaṃ vaktṛtvāt / vaidharmyeṇodāharaṇam - yatrāvītarāgatvaṃ nāsti, na sa vaktā / yathā - upalakhaṇḍa iti / yadyapyupalakhaṇḍādubhayaṃ vyāvṛtta tathāpi sarvo vītarāgo na vakteti vyāptyā vyatiraikāsiddheravyatirakaḥ /
3/134 apradarśitavyatireko yathā- anityaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvādākāśavaditi vaidharmyeṇa /
3/135 viparītavyatireko yathā- yadakṛtaka tannityaṃ bhavatīti
3/136 na hyebhirdṛṣṭāntābhāsairhetoḥ sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ sapakṣa eva sattvaṃ vipakṣo ca sarvatrāsattvameva niścayena śakyaṃ darśayituṃ viśeṣalakṣaṇaṃ vā / tadarthāpattyaiṣāṃ nirāso draṣṭavyaḥ /
3/137 dūṣaṇā nyūnatādyuktiḥ /
3/138 ye pūrvaṃ nyūnatādayaḥ sādhanadoṣā uktāsteṣāmudbhāvanaṃ dūṣaṇam / tena pareṣṭārthasiddhipratibandhāt /
3/139 dūṣaṇābhāsāstu jātayaḥ /
3/140 abhūtadoṣodbhāvanāni jātyuttaraṇīti /

3/1 Inference for another (<s>parārthānumāna</s>) is the statement of a three-form mark (<s>trirūpaliṅga</s>).
3/2 [This is so] because of the secondary application of the term 'effect' (<s>kārya</s>) to its cause (<s>kāraṇa</s>).
3/3 It is of two kinds,
3/4 on account of the difference in formulation (<s>prayogabheda</s>):
3/5 [namely,] the argument by way of similarity (<s>sādharmyavat</s>) and [the argument] by way of dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmyavat</s>).
3/6 Between the two there is no distinction in meaning (<s>arthatas</s>),
3/7 other than the difference in formulation.
3/8 Among these, the formulation of the argument by similarity: 'Whatever is accessible to the mark of perceptibility (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta</s>), yet is not perceived, is established as the object of a convention of non-existence (<s>asat</s>)' — for example, some other [pot] that has been seen; 'yet the pot, [which is] accessible to the mark of perceptibility, is not perceived in that particular place' — this is the formulation of non-perception (<s>anupalabdhi</s>).
3/9 Likewise the formulation of the natural property reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>): 'Whatever exists is impermanent, like a pot etc.' — this is the formulation of the pure natural property reason.
3/10 'Whatever is produced (<s>utpattimat</s>) is impermanent' — this is the formulation of the natural property by means of distinguishing [it as] a natural property-qualified characteristic.
3/11 'Whatever is made (<s>kṛtaka</s>) is impermanent' — [this is] by means of distinguishing a [necessary] condition (<s>upādhi</s>).
3/12 For a thing that depends on the operation of something external in bringing about its own nature is 'made' (<s>kṛtaka</s>).
3/13 Similarly, [formulations by] 'preceded by effort,' 'conditioned by a proximate cause,' 'differentiated in nature' and so forth are also to be understood.
3/14 'Sound exists, or is produced, or is made' — this is a demonstration of the property of the subject (<s>pakṣadharmopadarśana</s>).
3/15 All these probative properties (<s>sādhanadharmā</s>) are to be understood — each as proven by means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) — as concomitant only with the probative property in the property to be proven, [each] in its own domain.
3/16 Because that [property to be proven] is of the very same nature as [the probative property].
3/17 And because that nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) acts as the reason (<s>hetu</s>).
3/18 In reality, these two have identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) [with each other].
3/19 Because, when that [nature] has not arisen, [the entity] has not yet arisen; [therefore] it does not have that nature.
3/20 And because deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) would be possible [otherwise].
3/21 The formulation of the effect reason (<s>kāryahetu</s>): 'Where there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen etc.; and smoke is present here.'
3/22 Here too, when the causal relation (<s>kāryakāraṇabhāva</s>) has been established, the effect reason should be stated when the cause is what is to be proven.
3/23 The formulation of the argument by dissimilarity: 'Whatever is existent and accessible to the mark of perceptibility is perceived, as [in the case of] a blue patch etc.; yet the pot that is accessible to the mark of perceptibility as something existent is not perceived here' — this is the formulation of non-perception.
3/24 'If [sound] were permanent, it would lack existence, production, or being-made; but sound does exist and is produced and is made' — this is the formulation of the natural property reason.
3/25 'If fire were absent, there would certainly be no smoke; but smoke is present here' — this is the formulation of the effect reason.
3/26 For in the formulation by way of similarity, by implication the route of dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmyagati</s>) [is established].
3/27 Because when that [similar instance] is absent, the positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) of the reason with the property to be proven is absent.
3/28 Likewise, even in formulation by dissimilarity, the route of positive concomitance (<s>anvayagati</s>) [is established].
3/29 Because when that [dissimilar instance] is absent — [i.e.,] when the property to be proven is absent — the absence of the reason is not established.
3/30 For without a real essential connection (<s>svabhāvapratibandha</s>), the absence of one does not by necessity entail the absence of the other.
3/31 And that [connection] is of two kinds, as has been stated: characterized by identity (<s>tādātmyalakṣaṇa</s>) and characterized by causal origination (<s>tadutpattilakṣaṇa</s>).
3/32 And [thus] one who states the [counter-]exclusion must demonstrate the connection; therefore, the statement of exclusion is itself the demonstration of the implied connection. And demonstrating the connection is itself the statement of positive concomitance. Therefore, with either a single statement formulated by the route of positive concomitance or by the route of negative concomitance, the presence and absence of the mark in the <s>sapakṣa</s> (similar) and <s>asapakṣa</s> (dissimilar) [instances] has been stated — so a two-sentence formulation is not obligatory.
3/33 Even in [the case of] non-perception — when it has been said 'whatever is existent and accessible to the mark of perceptibility is certainly perceived,' the positive concomitance (<s>anvayasiddhi</s>) is established [by inference] that what is not perceived though of that kind is non-existent.
3/34 In both of these formulations, the statement of the <s>pakṣa</s> (subject) is not obligatory.
3/35 Because even in the formulation by similarity, when it is said 'whatever is accessible to the mark of perceptibility yet not perceived is an object of the convention of non-existence; and the pot, accessible to the mark of perceptibility, is not perceived here,' by force [of the argument] alone it follows that 'there is no pot here.'
3/36 Likewise, in the formulation by dissimilarity, when it is said 'what is an object of the convention of existence and accessible to the mark of perceptibility is certainly perceived; and such a pot of that kind is not perceived here,' by force alone it follows 'there is no object of the convention of existence here.'
3/37 What kind of <s>pakṣa</s> (subject/thesis), then, is to be stated?
3/38 The <s>pakṣa</s> is what is intended by the speaker himself, in its own form, and not refuted.
3/39 'In its own form' means: intended as what is to be proven (<s>sādhyatva</s>).
3/40 'In its own form alone' means: intended only as what is to be proven, not also as what proves (<s>sādhanatva</s>).
3/41 For example, in the inference of impermanence in sound, if visual perceptibility (<s>cākṣuṣatva</s>) were the reason, [visual perceptibility] would become the property to be proven [because it is] unestablished in sound — it is not [here] intended as the property to be proven but only because it is stated as the probative [property].
3/42 'By himself' means: by the proponent.
3/43 'Who then states the evidence.'
3/44 By this [phrase] it is stated: even if [the proponent] states the evidence while standing within some [particular] treatise, [and] even if the author of that treatise has accepted many properties in that subject, only that property which at that moment the proponent himself intends to prove is the property to be proven — not any other.
3/45 'Intended' means: even if not explicitly stated, [the property] is the thing to be proven where the evidence is presented by one who desires its establishment — the subject of the dispute.
3/46 Because the dispute has it as its referent.
3/47 For example: 'The eyes and other [sense organs] serve another's purposes because they are aggregates, like a bed, seat, and other body parts.' Here, even without stating 'serving the self' (<s>ātmārtha</s>), serving the self alone is what is to be proven. By this it is stated: not only what is explicitly stated is the property to be proven.
3/48 'Not refuted' — in order to show that even if what one intends to prove satisfies this characterization, if the intended property is refuted by direct perception, inference, well-known convention, or one's own statement, it is not the <s>pakṣa</s>.
3/49 Among these, refuted by direct perception, for example: 'Sound is not heard.' (1)
3/50 Refuted by inference, for example: 'Sound is permanent.' (2)
3/51 Refuted by conventional knowledge, for example: 'The moon is without a hare [on it].' (3)
3/52 Refuted by one's own statement, for example: 'Inference is not a means of valid knowledge.' (4)
3/53 Thus four pseudo-theses (<s>pakṣābhāsa</s>) are [here] stated and refuted.
3/54 Thus, what is already established, what [though not established] is considered by [someone else] a means of proof, what the proponent himself does not at that moment wish to prove, what is merely explicitly stated, and what is refuted — in contrast to these, [the thesis] as intended by the proponent in that very form, desired and not refuted, is [the definition]: thus the unimpeachable definition of the <s>pakṣa</s> has been demonstrated.
3/55 'Inference for another is the statement of a three-form mark' — this has been said. Among these, if even one of the three forms is absent, it is a pseudo-probans (<s>sādhanābhāsa</s>).
3/56 Even when stated, [there is a pseudo-probans] when [the three forms] are unestablished or doubtful with respect to the thing to be demonstrated and the demonstrator.
3/57 A <s>hetvābhāsa</s> (pseudo-reason, fallacy) [arises when] one form — the connection of the property to the subject — is either unestablished or doubtful in being unestablished.
3/58 For example: [In the inference] 'Sound is impermanent,' [the reason] 'visual perceptibility' is unestablished in both [parties].
3/59 [In the inference] 'Trees are conscious' [in order to prove] 'death upon complete removal of bark,' [the reason] 'death' is unestablished for the opponent — because he accepts death as characterized by the cessation of the faculties of cognition, sense organs, and life-force, and that is impossible in trees.
3/60 [In the inference] 'Pleasure and pain are non-conscious' [intended to prove this], [the reason] 'being produced' or 'being impermanent' is unestablished for the Sāṃkhya proponent himself.
3/61 Likewise, unestablishment [occurs] also when there is doubt about one's own relation to [the subject].
3/62 For example: when the aggregate of elements is doubtful [as to whether it takes the form of] mist etc., [that aggregate] is a sandigdhāsiddha (doubtfully unestablished reason) when indicated as the evidence for the establishment of fire.
3/63 As [in the case]: 'A peacock is crying in the thicket here.'
3/64 [This is so] in the confusion of the place of a [mere] reflected appearance.
3/65 [The reason is] also unestablished when the subject itself is unestablished — for example, [in the inference] 'the self is omnipresent' [in order to prove] the property 'having qualities that are perceived everywhere.'
3/66 Likewise, a pseudo-reason of inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikahetvābhāsa</s>) [arises when] one form — the absence [of the reason] in all dissimilar instances — is unestablished.
3/67 For example: [in the inference of] a property like impermanence in sound, a property like 'being an object of knowledge' (<s>prameyatva</s>) [which] occurs in all or in [only] a part of similar and dissimilar instances.
3/68 Likewise, even when doubtful regarding this very form, [there is] also an inconclusive [pseudo-reason].
3/69 For example: [in the inference] 'A specific person intended [to be described] is not omniscient, or has a king etc.' — [the property] 'being a speaker' (<s>vaktṛtva</s>) etc. has a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances.
3/70 Because a non-perception of the type 'an omniscient speaker is not perceived' is a cause of doubt, being directed at an imperceptible self — hence the exclusion of 'being a speaker' etc. from non-omniscients is doubtful.
3/71 And because there is no contradiction between speaking and omniscience, even if 'an omniscient is not a speaker' is not seen, the counter-exclusion is not established, due to doubt.
3/72 For the contradiction of entities is of two kinds.
3/73 [First,] the route of contradiction [occurs] when, of a cause with all its conditions complete, [the entity] is absent when the other [entity] is present — as in [the mutual] contradiction of cold and hot touch.
3/74 [Second,] by being characterized by mutually excluding positions, as in the case of existence and non-existence.
3/75 But neither of these two kinds of contradiction obtains between speaking and omniscience.
3/76 Nor is there a route to absence through non-perception of what is not incompatible.
3/77 Because the causal relation between passion (<s>rāga</s>) etc. and speech has not been established.
3/78 And the cessation of speech does not follow from the cessation of another entity that is not its cause.
3/79 Thus 'being a speaker' etc. is an inconclusive [pseudo-reason] with doubtful counter-exclusion.
3/80 The [pseudo-reason is] contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>) when the opposite [of the property to be proven] is established in the two [remaining] forms.
3/81 Which two [forms]?
3/82 The presence [of the reason] in the <s>sapakṣa</s>, and the absence [of the reason] in the <s>asapakṣa</s> — for example, 'being-made' (<s>kṛtatva</s>) and 'preceded by effort' are pseudo-reasons of the contradictory type [in the inference of] permanence in sound.
3/83 For these two have their opposite established: absence in the <s>sapakṣa</s> and presence in the <s>asapakṣa</s>.
3/84 And these two are contradictory because they prove the opposite of what is to be proven.
3/85 But does not a third also exist — a contradictory [pseudo-reason] that destroys one's own desired [thesis]?
3/86 For example: 'The eyes and other [sense organs] serve another's purposes because they are aggregates, like a bed, seat, and other body parts.'
3/87 [This is] contradictory because it proves the opposite of the unacknowledged desired property — [namely, it proves] that aggregates serve another's purpose [rather than that the self exists].
3/88 Why is this not stated here?
3/89 Because it falls under these two [types].
3/90 For this does not differ from those two in being a proof of the opposite of [one's] desired [thesis].
3/91 Because there is no distinction between 'desired' and 'explicitly stated' insofar as they are [both] what is to be proven.
3/92 [Pseudo-reason of] inconclusiveness [arises] when one of the two forms is unestablished and [there is] doubt about the other.
3/93 For example: '[A certain person is] free from passion (<s>vītarāga</s>), or omniscient, because of being a speaker etc.' — the counter-exclusion here is unestablished; the positive concomitance is doubtful.
3/94 The presence or absence of speech etc. in omniscience and freedom from passion is doubtful due to their being widely separated.
3/95 [Pseudo-reason of inconclusiveness arises also] when these very two forms are both doubtful.
3/96 For example: 'A living body has a self because it has prāṇa (<s>prāṇādimat</s>) etc.'
3/97 For there is no mass other than those with a self and those without a self, in which prāṇa etc. could exist.
3/98 Because everything is included by the delimitation of self as present or absent.
3/99 Nor is there certainty about the presence [of prāṇa] in either of these two [classes].
3/100 Because prāṇa etc. are not established as either having a self or lacking a self.
3/101 Therefore, prāṇa etc., related to a living body, are not established as excluded from everything that has a self and from everything that lacks a self — hence they are not excluded from either of them.
3/102 And they do not positively concomit with either.
3/103 Not even with a single self — because [that] too is unestablished.
3/104 Nor is there certainty of the positive or negative concomitance of that [reason] with what has a self or lacks a self.
3/105 Because certainty about the absence of one entails certainty about the presence of the other as its necessary consequence.
3/106 And because positive concomitance and counter-exclusion have the form of mutually exclusive delimitation — hence, due to the doubt about positive and counter concomitance, [this is] inconclusive.
3/107 Because of the absence of certainty about either the property to be proven or the other.
3/108 Thus, when each or any two of the three forms is either unestablished or doubtful, the three pseudo-reasons of unestablishment (<s>asiddha</s>), contradiction (<s>viruddha</s>), and inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntika</s>) [arise] as appropriate.
3/109 A mutually exclusionary non-deviating [reason] (<s>viruddhāvyabhicārin</s>) has also been mentioned as a cause of doubt. Why is it not stated here?
3/110 Because it is impossible in the domain of inference.
3/111 For there is no possibility of contradiction between an effect and a natural property characterized as stated, and non-perception.
3/112 And there is no other non-deviating [but contradictory reason].
3/113 Therefore, a contradictory non-deviating probative defect has been mentioned with respect to [inferences that] proceed on the basis of seeing what is not real, relying on scripture — [but] in the investigation of those meanings:
3/114 Because it is possible that authors of treatises, by confusion, present [a reason of] contrary nature with respect to their intended meanings.
3/115 For this is not possible in the perception of the nature of things as they actually stand, [when they are] non-perceptions of effects of the self.
3/116 Its example: 'Whatever is co-apprehended simultaneously by all its related entities stationed everywhere is omnipresent, like ether; and the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is co-apprehended simultaneously by all entities stationed everywhere related to it.'
3/117 The state of having its own-nature present at that place is [merely] a concomitant of being a nature related to that [entity].
3/118 For it is not the case that what is not present somewhere pervades that place by its own self — thus [it is] a formulation of the natural property reason.
3/119 A second formulation: 'Whatever is existent and accessible to the mark of perceptibility is certainly present there; but the universal, accessible to the mark of perceptibility as something existent, is not perceived in the intervals between individuals.' This non-perception and [this] natural property, by proving objects of mutually contradictory [theses] in a single case, generate doubt.
3/120 A three-form reason has been stated. Yet a cognition of the object is not [produced] by that alone — therefore, no separate entity called the 'example' (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) is a constituent of the probans; therefore its definition is not stated separately, since its meaning is already covered.
3/121 The property of the reason — presence only in the <s>sapakṣa</s> and complete absence from the <s>asapakṣa</s> — has been stated as a single [composite] form [above]. Moreover, specifically, for the causal and natural property [reasons] characterized as stated, the concomitance of origination and nature alone must be shown — and they have been stated; and in showing them: 'Where there is smoke, there is fire; and when fire is absent, there is certainly no smoke anywhere, as in [the case of] a kitchen [versus other places]; where there is being-made, there is impermanence; and when impermanence is absent, being-made is impossible, as in [the case of] a pot [versus] ether' — this must be shown. For otherwise one cannot show — in the manner stated — the presence and absence of the mark in similar and dissimilar instances. That invariable concomitance (<s>niyama</s>) with the effect [for the] effect-mark, and the pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) by nature for the nature-mark — once this matter is shown, the examples are shown; since they are of that very form.
3/122 By this very [argument] the defects of examples (<s>dṛṣṭāntadoṣa</s>) are also dismissed.
3/123 For example: 'Sound is permanent because it is non-material, like action, or like a paramāṇu (atom), or like a pot' — these are pseudo-examples (<s>dṛṣṭāntābhāsa</s>) lacking both the property to be proven and the probative property.
3/124 Likewise, those with a doubtful property to be proven and so forth — for example: 'This person has passion, because of speaking, like the person on the street.' 'This person has the nature of being subject to death, because of having passion, like the person on the street.' 'This person is not omniscient because of having passion, like the person on the street.'
3/125 Likewise, [examples with] absence of positive concomitance or a positive concomitance not demonstrated — for example: 'One who speaks has passion, as in the case of the desired [person].' 'Sound is impermanent because it is made, like a pot.'
3/126 Likewise, inverted positive concomitance — 'Whatever is impermanent is made.'
3/127 These are the defects of the example by way of similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>).
3/128 By way of dissimilarity also: 'Like a paramāṇu, like an action, like ether' — those that are non-departing from the property to be proven etc.
3/129 Likewise, those with a doubtful departure from the property to be proven etc. — for example: '[The teachers] <s>Kapila</s> etc. are not omniscient, or are not trustworthy (<s>āpta</s>), because [their] teaching has not the mark of a valid cognition manifesting omniscient trustworthiness.' Here the dissimilar example: 'Whoever is omniscient or trustworthy taught the knowledge of light etc., like <s>Ṛṣabha</s>, <s>Vardhamāna</s> etc.' In this, the departure of the property to be proven — non-omniscience and non-trustworthiness — is doubtful.
3/130 [An example with a] doubtful departure of the probative property — for example: '[A particular person] should not be given credence by the follower of the three Vedas (<s>trayīvidyā</s>) as a Brahmin, because of having passion etc.' Here the dissimilar example: 'Those who are worthy of credence do not have passion, like <s>Gautama</s> etc., the composers of the <s>dharmaśāstra</s>s.' The departure of the probative property — passion — from <s>Gautama</s> etc. is doubtful.
3/131 [An example with a] doubtful departure of both — for example: '<s>Kapila</s> etc. are not free from passion, because of possessing acceptance and non-acceptance of possessions.' Here the dissimilar example: 'Whoever is free from passion does not have acceptance and non-acceptance of possessions, like <s>Ṛṣabha</s> etc.' The departure of the properties to be proven and proven — non-freedom-from-passion and possession-of-acceptance-and-non-acceptance — from <s>Ṛṣabha</s> etc. is doubtful.
3/132 [An example with] absence of departure — for example: 'This [person] is not free from passion because he is a speaker.' The dissimilar example: 'Where there is no non-freedom-from-passion, there is no speaker, like a stone.' Although both are excluded from the stone, the departure is not established because of the pervasion that every non-free-from-passion is not a speaker; hence absence of departure.
3/133 [An example where departure is] not shown — for example: 'Sound is impermanent because of being made, like ether' in the dissimilar [formulation].
3/134 Inverted departure — for example: 'Whatever is not made is permanent.'
3/135 For by these pseudo-examples, it is impossible to show with certainty the generic characteristic — presence only in the <s>sapakṣa</s> and complete absence in all the <s>asapakṣa</s> — or the specific characteristic. Their dismissal is to be understood [as proceeding] by the implication of these meanings.
3/136 Refutation (<s>dūṣaṇa</s>) is a statement of the deficiency and the rest.
3/137 Refutation is the articulation of the deficiencies and other defects of the probans stated above — thereby blocking the establishing of the meaning desired by the other [party].
3/138 But pseudo-refutations (<s>dūṣaṇābhāsa</s>) are the <s>jāti</s>-rejoinders.
3/139 <s>Jāti</s>-rejoinders are [those] that articulate non-existent defects.
Thus (ends) the third chapter, the Examination of Inference for Others (<s>parārthānumānaparicchedaḥ</s>).
The <s>Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa</s> (Treatise on the Drop of Logic) is completed.
